toc.title: Listen mindfully to your body's needs

q: "Once the passive pathway effectively shifts our physiological state, the second step can be initiated. Exercising the vagal brake recruits the active voluntary pathway through rituals requiring manipulation of breath, posture, and vocalization." (Porges)

blocks.p: We've discussed the basics of safety and the external environment. Passive safety comes first: [changes in your environment](piece:anchor-environment) that bring you passive safety cues. Now, we're going to actively build on that foundation. Once neurocepting safety cues passively from the environment, you can use active means to feel safety, even anchoring into it. We'll focus on movement as one avenue for active safety anchoring.

At this stage, our focus remains on establishing safety rather than confronting defensive responses. Though movement can effectively release stuck defensive activation, that work comes later: only after you've built a strong foundation of safety and developed curiosity about your inner experiences. Once you're curious, then you could intentionally feel into stuck defense and use movement as a means to release it.

Our bodies are always prepared to do something, even when immobile. Like right now, you're immobile but might be fidgeting with something. Or you might be bouncing your leg. If not, your eyes are scanning this page. If you chose to stop reading, your eyes would still scan the environment, pulled unconsciously toward whatever is the most compelling. And, of course, you're breathing, so your torso is moving to some degree.

Both the degree and flavor of mobility change depending on our state. Each state brings different impulses for movement. If we're in a flight state, we have an impulse to run. If we're in a fight state, we have an impulse to lean forward in aggression. From safety, we have impulses to move our face into a smile or get closer to someone and use touch. These are all varying degrees of movement, each with a different look and feel.

I invite you to become more aware of your body's movements and their flavor. These can be movements you naturally or typically do without thinking of, like typing the words to a book on building your Polyvagal safety state (which we all do, right?). Your movements can also be ones you choose to do, like dancing. Movement might be overwhelming, so let's break it down into size categories to help you manage what you notice.

Large movements are exactly what they sound like. These can get you moving from one spot to another. Or movements that use force and power. These might be dancing, running, push-ups, or even pushing against a wall.

Large movements are great for flight/fight activation. They can also be a good fit if you're unthawing a freeze state and flight/fight is attempting to discharge. Large movements are ideal for high energy play as well.

Large movements may not suit you if you exist in a shutdown state. In shutdown, there is an impulse to immobilize, isolate, and reduce stimulation. In shutdown, you don't have the mobilization necessary to use large movements, like running or boxing. But you may acquire mobilization as you exit from shutdown into sympathetic.

My favorite large muscle movements involve swimming. I love diving into the water, gliding through it, or kicking off the pool's walls. These movements provide me with a sense of power and focus. When I'm in an aggressive fight energy state, I use my hands to push against the resistance of the water. When experiencing flight energy, I utilize my legs by kicking off the wall or treading water. During shutdown, I like less movement, preferring to hold my breath underwater, taking in the muted and dull ambiance. And in safety, I play spontaneously in the pool with my kids.

Medium movements will still use your larger muscles but require less force and potentially less movement from space to space. Medium movements could be good for exiting shutdown and welcoming sympathetic energy back into your system. They may also act as a slow and deliberate container or avenue for flight/fight energy.

You could squeeze your hand into a fist instead of pushing against a wall (large). Instead of dancing across the room, you might walk up and down the hall. Medium movements may encompass purposeful and slower gestures and positions, like in yoga and tai chi practices. While they engage the whole body, they don't involve big, forceful, powerful motions.

Small movements basically involve staying in place. These actions are much smaller in scale and are very discreet. These may include wiggling your toes, looking around to orient yourself, rolling your head, or fidgeting with something. A small movement might be tilting your head toward the sky to see the night stars. It could also be reaching out and holding your partner's hand.

Active safety cues serve multiple possible benefits. They can help you cope with defense or anchor in safety through mindfulness. And they can eventually help you to climb your Polyvagal ladder and even discharge stuck defensive state activation as self-regulation impulses arise. Just like environmental cues, mindfulness is absolutely imperative in shifting an active movement cue into a safety anchor (as well as the other Anchoring Potentials we will explore).

For example, fidgeting alone is merely fidgeting. If you don't consciously attune to the sensations of fidgeting and notice what it feels like, you won't truly experience it: you'll simply go through the motions. Fidgeting without mindfulness can still serve a purpose, like helping you focus on a lesson you are listening to. It acts as a coping skill or a way to manage mobilization. But when done mindfully, it can help anchor you into your safety state. And eventually, you can use mindful fidgeting to climb your Polyvagal ladder actively.
If you don't approach these safety cues mindfully, nothing will change. However, by mindfully attuning to them, you can facilitate anchoring in your safety state.

So, direct your focus to the experience of the movements you develop. Pay attention to how they make you feel in your emotions and sensations; notice muscle relaxation before, during, and after your practices. Notice how your breathing changes when using movement. Notice which ones bring you closer to a smile or further from one. Notice what you generally like and dislike, then focus more time and energy on the ones you like.

Breath is a small to medium movement that happens spontaneously. But you can also control your breath consciously. At this point, I don't recommend you direct your breath. Simply allow your breath to follow its natural course.

I'll tell you the same thing I tell my clients: "Your body knows what it needs more than your brain does." Your body may breathe tightly into the chest due to sympathetic activation. That's what it needs. But your brain may tell you, "That's not the right way to breathe. I should use the box breathing method and use my senses through the 54321 method and bilaterally stimulate myself and journal how I feel…" Stop. Don't control.

Instead, observe and be present with it. If your lungs need a deep inhalation, allow and observe it. If your breath naturally goes into your belly, allow and observe it. If you're breathing tightly into your chest, allow and observe it. At least for a moment. I find that the breath naturally adjusts on its own once we meet it where it's at. Be an observer and mindfully experience what your body is doing. (Your breath likely made an adjustment after you read this paragraph and simply became aware of your breathing.)

However, if this is uncomfortable and you prefer prescribed breathing techniques, that's fine, too. But ask yourself if you are trying to control or if you are curious about your experience. If you try color breathing, is it because you're curious about the experience? Or is it because you are trying to control something? Are you trying to make your emotions go away? Or are you experimenting with breath to settle into safety? Experimenting with breath for the sake of curiosity can serve as a small to medium movement cue. If you're controlling your breathing to make an emotion go away, that's not safety cueing. That sounds like coping.

As you practice allowing your natural breath, you'll become better at noticing how various safety cues cause your breathing to adjust naturally. If you can breathe comfortably and fully into your belly, that's a great indication that your safety state is active.

Notice where your breath goes into your body as you're reading this. (Yes, I know, it goes into your lungs.) When you breathe in and out, what do you notice moving? Does your chest expand? Your belly? Do your shoulders move?
This little exercise can help you to get more in touch with your breath. Don't try to change it; just notice what your body naturally needs and does.

Very commonly, wellness "experts" on social media advocate using some technique to "activate," "stimulate," or "hack" your vagus nerve. I've seen these evangelists hyping things like gargling, splashing cold water on your face, swimming in a freezing cold ocean, rubbing some part of your neck, craning your neck in a very distorted uncomfortable-looking position, or putting a bag of frozen peas on your chest. In all fairness, you may find some of these techniques helpful. If so, use them. It is not the activities themselves that concern me.

I'm concerned that you will be repeatedly misled by false promises of a shortcut or quick fix. I'm concerned that you will endlessly follow the recommendations of popular influencers on TikTok instead of taking the time to learn to listen to the innate wisdom of your own body. It's out of these concerns that I implore you not to get caught up in searching for the "right" technique. It's more important to me that you focus on how you feel in response to what you're doing. In other words, mindfully experience the activity and ask yourself: "Do I feel safer or not?"

These social media tricks are typically not promises of safety. These are intended to reduce defensive activation, which is fine. But reducing defense is not the same as increasing safety. These are mindless coping options at best; not safety cues or anchors.

Gussy met with me for a 1:1 Coaching session. He had put "the work" into his healing process, including enrolling in and taking an online course designed to heal his nervous system through movement. (Or was it "reset" or "tune"? It doesn't matter…) He said he liked some of the exercises he learned about, but was not seeing the progress he would like. His pesky freeze activation was still showing up at inopportune moments, like seeing friends.

I asked him about his safety practices, as he had some knowledge of the Polyvagal Theory, having followed my content for a while on the podcast. He told me one of the exercises he likes is laying on his back and rolling around.
"What do you like about it?" I asked. (When my clients tell me they use a specific exercise or breathing technique, I always ask this. I'm trying to figure out the intention behind their exercises.)
"Because it feels good," he said.
"'Good' meaning what?"
"'Good' like it helps contain my anxiety," Gussy said.

I have no doubt that the nervous system healing/resetting/tuning exercise (perhaps even some "brain rewiring" or "dopamine stimulation"? Who the heck knows?) might have indeed felt "good" for Gussy. But you can probably see a couple issues here, dear reader -

ol: The "right" movement: Gussy was following a prescribed movement. He used that movement because an expert told him to, without regard for what his body actually needed to access safety. He checked a box instead of being mindful of his experience and asking himself if he felt safe or not.

Intention: Gussy wasn't accessing safety; he was at best containing anxiety. His intention was to reduce defense, not increase safety. While understandable, if the goal is to reduce defense, you're not going to mindfully experience and look for safety. Instead of prioritizing defense reduction, seek safety experiences and the byproduct will be a reduction in defense. Intention matters.

blocks.p: It's totally fine to use the various and random hacks and stimulators and whatnot that you find online. But when you try these movements out, please listen mindfully to your body's experience. Does it feel safer or not? Less defense is not the same as more safety, though more safety leads to less defense.

blocks.h: Listen mindfully to your body's needs

blocks.p: Approach all of this with curiosity. When it comes to movements, pay attention to how your body naturally wants to move. Explore what actions or movements help you feel more grounded, breathe easier, and connect with your external surroundings. Be curious about everything you do. If you're going for a walk, approach it with curiosity. If you're pushing a shopping cart, be present and curious about that experience. The same goes for tai chi movements or squeezing a fidget toy.

I have no idea if pushing against a wall will help you. It is more likely to help you if you're in a fight state and less likely to be helpful if you're in a shutdown state. But in your fight state, you may hate pushing against a wall and prefer pushing into your palms. Depending on your current state, there are likely multiple appropriate movements and actions that can be effective. I don't know which ones will work best for you, and you may not know either. Prioritize mindfully experiencing some of these options, and then gauge whether they bring you closer to safety.

Focus on the experience of what you are doing, not so much the outcome of it. Of course, the outcome is important. You're reading this for a reason. There is a goal that you want to achieve. But to reach the goal, you must first listen to the present-moment experience of what your body is doing.

As you experiment with various body movements, pay attention to the present moment experience of using them. Focusing on the present is much different than using some technique to get an end result. Look at these two examples and notice the difference:

ol: Jen wants to get rid of her anxiety, so she uses a "vagal nerve hack" of placing a frozen bag of peas on her chest, thinking it is "activating her vagus nerve."
Randall is curious about how pushing into his palms would feel, so he tries it out and pays attention to whether his body has more of a like or dislike sensation.

blocks.p: As you can see, these are very different experiences. Jen desires to rid herself of a valid experience she is having. Randall is curious about the experience of a particular action. Randall could very well identify that pushing into his palms results in a feeling of like. He could then add this to a varied menu of effective safety anchors to continue practicing as part of his daily routine or as needed to reduce fight activation. Jen will likely attempt the same bag of peas technique repeatedly in a desperate attempt to rid herself of her anxiety. (BTW, she might be inadvertently activating her dorsal vagal shutdown system in her desperate attempt to stop her sympathetic activation.)

Curiosity drives Randall's experience. He may have a result in mind to reduce his anger. But he needs to focus on his present experience to achieve the result. As you identify and practice potential safety anchors, including the ones that use movement, start from curiosity as best you can. Don't wait for a panic attack to try something out, like Jen does with the frozen pea bag.

As you practice, you'll notice how a certain movement generally causes you to feel. But over time, you'll identify how that same movement causes you to feel, depending on your state. For example, when you try pushing on your palms in a fight state, it's probably a better experience than in a shutdown state. For now, focus on what is generally a like or dislike.
Let's review what your body might need depending on what state it's in. Remember: these are merely ideas and generalities. It's up to you to experiment and rule in or out what is or isn't helpful.

In shutdown, there is an impulse to immobilize and often to be alone with minimal stimulation. Keep this in mind as you try out different sizes of body movements. If you exist in primarily a shutdown state, medium and large movements may not "feel" right. Instead, you will probably sense a pull towards smaller movements.

Use these smaller movements in an environment that is conducive to lower stimulation. Lower stimulation environments have dimmer lighting and a place to sit quietly in mostly silence. Your chosen environment might be [the safety environment you set up](piece:anchor-environment). But it could very well be outside. Pick an environment that feels more right than not, then allow yourself to immobilize.

Allowing yourself to immobilize might seem counterintuitive, given this piece's focus on movement and body anchors. But that is likely what you need from a shutdown state. As you allow immobilization, then become curious about what movements might feel right. Start very small, like with your eyes or toes.

In shutdown, using your eyes to reorient to the environment can be helpful. You could purposefully look around the room, or you could just immobilize and allow your eyes to carry your attention to where they like. Your eyes will naturally shift toward whatever is pulling their attention. Be curious about this process and witness what unfolds.

Wiggling your toes might also be a good option in a significant shutdown state. And if not your toes, perhaps your fingers. Pick a part of your body that you can begin to move from immobilization and notice if you like it or dislike it. As you follow what feels more right than not, you may see some mobility returning to your system.

Another option you always have available to you is noticing your breath. Don't try to change it. Allow your lungs to breathe in the way that they naturally need to. It will probably be shallow, with long gaps between deflation and the next inhalation, which is common in shutdown. Let yourself be immobilized and focus on the movement of your natural breathing.

Another small movement potential for shutdown is flexing. Flexing reminds your muscles they're still active and can move. If you can handle toe wiggles, you can probably handle this. Try flexing various muscles and see if anything feels right. Don't look for trauma discharges; instead, look for what is tolerable, possible, or maybe even pleasurable.

Fidgets can be a good option for shutdown as well. But you won't be fidgeting to direct flight/fight activation. Fidgeting in shutdown is more about the sensory experience. So instead of "fidgets," let's call them "sensorgets." "Sensoryets"? Never mind, let's just call them "fidgets" still.

Fidgeting in shutdown is naturally slower, so let it be slower. When you fidget, allow and notice the slowness. Experience what it's like to slowly and deliberately move your thumb across whatever you're holding. It could be a fidget, but it could also be a blanket on your couch. Or the couch itself. Or the insides of your pockets.

If you're in a collapsed state and lacking energy, allow that. Let your body reconnect to the environment through small movements. Use your eyes. Use your fingers. Remind your body it can move through toe wiggles. Follow your breathing. And then try flexing your muscles. None of this involves moving from the place you're in. You can do this from your bed or your couch or the floor. You can do this in a dark, depressing room or a dim, cozy room (I recommend the latter). Don't judge it; just try it out without rejecting your shutdown state.

As you naturally emerge from immobility to mobility, you will notice energy coming back into your system. It could be as obvious as a surge in sympathetic activation and feeling inspired to go for a jog. But it could also be smaller, like remembering a chore you need to get done and feeling ready to do it. Or an idea may pop into your mind about a creative endeavor, like painting or gardening. Notice as these things pop into your mind or when your body is ready to get up and get moving.
From sympathetic mobility, there is an impulse to move. (Shocking, I know.) The mobility state can have many flavors to it:

The evasive and aggressive flavors of mobilization are more directly connected to a defensive state of flight or fight. This suggests a lack of safety in the system. If this describes your experience, get up and move. It may be the most beneficial thing you can do when leaning toward mobile defensive activation and away from safety. There is no one right movement, but it might feel good to briskly walk outside, do push-ups, or tense and then relax your muscles. No matter what you do, listen to the needs of your body and act on them. If you feel highly anxious, a faster walk is probably more helpful than a slower one. As you listen to the needs of your body and the flight/fight edge softens, then increase your mindfulness of the active experience and your passive surroundings.

Another possible mobility flavor is play, which can feel more like escape or aggression. Remember: play is the combination of the safety state along with the mobility state with a safe other. Playing in flight can feel like evasive exuberance, like running away from someone in a game of freeze tag. It can also be aggressive playfulness, like chasing after that same someone when it's your turn to be "it." Play also has safety within it, so there is an opportunity to be mindful of the excitement in another's voice and face during play.

The fight state will pull your body toward things involving power and force like pushing, lifting, and squeezing. These movements will use your upper body: arms, chest, and back muscles. Examples of potential fight movements are pushing against a wall, pushing into your palms, squeezing a towel, lifting weights, or punching a bag. Lingering aggressive mobility feels like anger or irritation; these can be good signs that your body needs some type of aggressive movement.

The flight state will pull you toward movements that create space. The flight energy of your body might compel you to go out on a walk, jog, or even sprint. Flight movements typically involve your legs or some means of getting space. You'll feel lingering escape mobility as anxiousness or worry; these can be good signs that your body needs some escape movement using your legs.

Creativity, productivity, and motivation are all energized, but must involve some level of safety. They're mobile, but the mobility is directed toward a specific task or goal, like working out, painting, or starting a new project. These safety flavors potentially require ideation, multi-step planning, critical thinking, sustained attention, patience, overcoming obstacles, spontaneously shifting goals when required, frustration tolerance, and even working with others. These things don't happen from the immobility of shutdown and they don't happen from defensive mobilization. These flavors of mobility are great opportunities to attach mindfulness to the experiences since they must involve significant safety state activation.

Mobility levels from creativity, productivity, and motivation will vary significantly. Working out in a gym has obvious movement involved. But painting may not be as obvious. Painting has smaller movements while working out has bigger movements. Gardening can have small movements, like pruning the leaves on a rose bush, but can also involve using all your muscles to pull at a pesky root.

Mobility has many flavors with varying levels of safety or danger. For now, be aware of potential defensive activation and what it may need, like walking briskly when anxious. But the focus should be on what helps you feel generally more connected to yourself, others, and the environment in the present moment. Try to focus on safety experiences and less on what helps to reduce defensive activation, though that is of course important, too.

In the safety state, you can access a wider range of movements. Safety plus flight/fight mobility results in play with a safe other or exercise when alone. Safety plus shutdown immobility results in intimacy with a safe other or stillness when alone. These safety hybrids will allow you to use all the movement sizes, from small to large.

Movements from safety won't be fear-driven; instead, they may feel like co-regulatory, connected, or fun experiences. Safety movements will likely feel more fluid, rhythmic, and spontaneous. As you practice your safety anchors and build your safety state, you will have more access to movements that utilize the other Polyvagal states as mixed states.
The safety state allows a wider range of movement, but it also may lead to connective movement. We can break this down into three potential connective movement types: self, others, and environment.

ul: Connection to self movement: Safety unlocks the ability to connect with yourself through movement. This involves the mindful experiencing of what it feels like to move. This will commonly utilize creative experiences, like dance, painting, or even the slight movements of stillness in self-reflection.

Connection to others movement: When with a safe other, your safety state will guide you toward them for safe connection. This can include hugs, handshakes, and even physical intimacy. On a much smaller scale, you may notice your eyes are pulled toward theirs or your face spontaneously creates a smile.

Connection to environment movement: Your safety state may pull you toward elements of the environment for connection. If you're walking around your block or a park, you may be pulled toward the shade of a large tree or the scent of a rose garden. When on a beach, you'll have the impulse to pick up sand and let it run through your fingers or sit and listen to the water.

blocks.p: If you can identify which movements align with your state, that's fantastic. It means you are ahead of the curve. However, recognizing one's current state can be challenging. It may require internal awareness that you may not have fully developed yet, and that's perfectly okay.

You should approach body movements as an experiment. Focus more on how your body responds to various movements instead of worrying about your state and where it's at on the Polyvagal ladder. Simply be curious and explore what feels good without worrying about your state.

For example, I mentioned pushing against a wall. I don't want you to ask yourself, "Am I in the right state to push against the wall?" Instead, I invite you to try it and ask yourself, "Does this feel right?" If it doesn't, try something else and ask again, "Does this feel right?"

One goal here is to create a menu of safety anchors. As you identify what movements feel good, add them to the list. Make a menu of movements (and other anchors) that you can refer to and practice. You can use this menu during dysregulation to help you cope. Eventually, this menu will be helpful to feel and release stuck trauma.
If you don't know what to notice, ask yourself these three questions when practicing movements or the other anchoring potentials -

ol: When I do _, am I more or less likely to smile?
Is my breathing more or less comfortable when I _?
Do my muscles get more or less tense when I _?

blocks.p: If you are more likely to smile, breath is more comfortable, and muscles reduce in tension, then you've got yourself a potentially great safety anchor. Put it on your list, keep practicing it, and experiment with others! As you build the strength of your safety state over time, the movements and other anchors will shift. What feels right now may not feel right a month from now. This process never stops; you should always be curious about what helps you feel safer than not.
Take a moment to notice your current body posture.

ul: How does it make you feel? Do you feel more connected, ready to take action, frozen, or inclined to hide in this posture?
Observe your breath. Is it primarily in your shoulders, chest, or belly?

blocks.p: Then, reflect on what is typical.

ul: Does your body typically prefer movement or immobility?
When it likes movement, what type brings your body feelings of safety? (Refer to your list of safety feelings.)
When it likes to be immobile, what does that look like?

blocks.p: Research different options for movement. Here are some starting points:

ul: Things people do to "feel better," to get some energy out, be more in the present moment, and feel safe.
Search for "physical grounding exercises," "moving meditation," or something similar.

blocks.p: Identify & list three movement types from your research that you will practice. I recommend practicing these for a while before moving on. Ask yourself the three questions to assess if it should be added to your list of potential safety anchors.

ol: Movement can be helpful for safety anchoring. To reduce overwhelm, think of movement in terms of size: small, medium, or large.
Mindfully use the various movement sizes without worrying about releasing stuck trauma. Focus on the present moment experience and identify whether you feel more or less safety.
Initially, focus on building a menu of potential movement anchors. Later, connect them to the corresponding Polyvagal states in which they may be most helpful based on your experience.

blocks.why: Movement as an anchor, at the size your body wants right now.

blocks.prompt: Did this provide you with any new experiences of safety?
Was this challenging for you? What about it was challenging?
Is this something you can continue to practice?
What three body movements had the most benefit? Did they have something in common?

blocks.p: Yeah. It might be scary.

Not just the movement-based anchors but the entire process of unstucking might be scary. We're focusing on safety here. But safety is just one phase in the overall process of getting unstuck from trauma. After this, you'll work on directly experiencing your stuck state. Well, if you want to, that is.
It's scary. We can validate that.

But fear is also a normal part of change. Any change, including and perhaps especially trauma recovery, and maybe especially if you have stuck freeze energy. (Fear comes with the immobilization of flight/fight.) But unstucking can generally feel intimidating and uncomfortable. It's common to have hesitancy in the process. Doubt too.
So, your fear is valid and it's normal.

Recognize that these feelings are natural. They occur as part of the process. For now, just let them be. Don't do anything with them except maybe validate and normalize their existence. Don't try to make them go away. They're there and they're real. Accept that as best you can for now and then continue to focus on your safety practices.

The fear is real and you're not going to fight it. In a sense, you're saying "hi" to it and then continuing on your way. You're almost giving it permission to be with you as you practice safety. If the fear is too much, do whatever coping skills you typically use, like distracting yourself with social media. As the fear lowers, then validate and normalize it, and even give it permission to hang out with you in your pocket (or on your shoulder or in a bag) as you practice safety.

The movement-based body anchors might be more challenging for you, probably depending on your path to getting stuck in a traumatized state. Don't take this as a sign that it's time to stop altogether. Again, validate and normalize that experience. If you need to, take a break from movement anchors and try [sensory anchors](piece:sensory-anchors). Your senses might be more approachable for you at this time.

Not all of these anchors may be accessible to you all at once. Instead, one of them may be easier for you. Start by practicing the one(s) that are more approachable. When you're ready, return to the ones that seem less approachable. Maximize what you can, then build on the rest. Your stronger foundation of safety will open the possibility of experimenting with the ones that were more challenging.
